text: This capstone starts the same way most real BI work does -- not as a fully scoped project, but as one sentence from one stakeholder.

You work in BI at Thornbury Cycle Supply Co, a reseller of Adventure Works Cycles products. The Merchandising Manager stops by and asks: can you show me how our product categories are doing this quarter, I want one dashboard I can pull up in the pricing review. Four words in that sentence are each hiding a real question. This quarter -- to date, or the full quarter? Categories -- category, subcategory, or individual product? How they're doing -- revenue, order count, or both? And one dashboard -- a quick glance in a meeting, or something kept open all quarter?

None of those are hard questions. They're just questions nobody's asked yet. A short follow-up conversation gets you four concrete answers: the time window, the scope, the metric, and the grouping -- before you touch a keyboard.

After that conversation, the vague ask becomes something specific: build a Power BI report showing total sales amount and order count for the current quarter, broken out by product category, for the Merchandising Manager to review ahead of the quarterly pricing review meeting. That's now a sentence you could hand to a teammate and get the same report back.

Scoping also means saying what's out of bounds. This project covers one quarter, every product category, in one Power BI report. It deliberately skips subcategory-level detail, any multi-quarter trend, and any pricing recommendation -- deciding what to do about pricing is what the meeting itself is for.
With the requirement written down, next lesson turns it into a plain-English plan for the T-SQL query -- which real tables this needs, and how they join together.
